# The Hidden Reason Plans, Budgets And Forecasts Fall Apart


Share:


- Copied!


-
-
-


Ask a finance chief how satisfied they are with their company's planning process, and the answer is rarely enthusiastic. According to the[2026 AFP FP&A Benchmarking Survey Report on integrated planning](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/training-resources/resources/survey-research-economic-data/Details/afp-fpabenchmarking-survey-report-integrated-planning) , based on responses from 332 finance professionals across 54 countries, the average corporate budgeting cycle still takes nearly nine weeks to complete, a figure that hasn't moved in three years despite widespread investment in new planning technology. The same research found that while 90% of finance teams actively manage risks and opportunities, far fewer formalize that work into an actual integrated planning process, and that alignment on the plan is strongest among executives while weakening sharply the further it travels down into operational teams.


That gap points to a problem that's structural rather than technological: Most companies run long-range planning, annual budgeting and rolling forecasting as three separate exercises, owned by overlapping but distinct groups, on different cycles, often built on different assumptions. When those three processes drift apart, which they do constantly, the result isn't just inefficiency. It's a company steering itself with three different maps that don't quite agree on where north is.


### Long Range and Annual Plans Exist to Enforce Strategy, not Predict the Future


The first thing to get right is what a long-range plan and an annual budget are for. Their job isn't to be accurate. Their job is to force a choice given limited capital, limited people and limited time, which handful of strategic bets is the company going to make, and how much is it willing to commit to each one. A five-year plan and a one-year budget are both, at their core, commitment devices, not forecasts.


That distinction matters because of a problem finance has struggled with for decades. Michael Jensen, the late Harvard Business School professor,[made the case in a widely cited Harvard Business Review article](https://hbr.org/2001/11/corporate-budgeting-is-broken-lets-fix-it) that using a single number for both target-setting and honest forecasting is close to self-defeating. When a manager's compensation depends on hitting a budget number, Jensen argued, that manager has every incentive to negotiate the number down in advance and then manage the business defensively once it's approved, rather than reporting what's likely to happen. A budget with incentives attached will always be biased toward being achievable rather than being accurate. That's a feature of a strategic commitment device, not a flaw, but it means the annual plan and the long-range plan can never also be relied on as an honest, up to date read of where the business is heading.


### Rolling Forecasts Exist to Tell the Truth


That's precisely the job a rolling forecast is built to do instead: give management an unbiased, continuously updated view of where the business is landing, independent of what anyone previously committed to hit.[Gartner's research on CFO priorities for 2026](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-08-12-gartner-survey-shows-top-priorities-for-cfos-in-2026-include-cost-optimization) found that 51% of finance chiefs now rank improving financial forecast accuracy and quality among their top five priorities, even as many of those same CFOs simultaneously navigate a stated tension between hitting cost targets and funding new growth. That tension is easier to manage when the forecast isn't also carrying the burden of being a target. A rolling forecast that's allowed to say "we're not going to hit plan" without political consequence is far more useful than one that's quietly smoothed to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.


This is where a lot of companies get the design wrong. They build the rolling forecast as a repeat of the budget exercise, updated monthly, using the same inputs, the same owners and often the same incentives baked in. That approach imports the budget's bias directly into the forecast, defeating the entire purpose of having two separate instruments in the first place.


### Why the First Year of the Long Range Plan Has to Match the Annual Budget


If long-range plans and annual budgets are both strategy-led commitment devices, they need to agree with each other, at least in the near term.[Research from The Hackett Group](https://www.thehackettgroup.com/the-hackett-group-digital-world-class-finance-teams-operate-at-45-lower-cost-and-deliver-faster-smarter-insights/) backs this up directly: Its 2025 benchmarking of Digital World Class finance organizations found that top-performing finance functions are 54% more likely than their peers to keep business planning genuinely aligned with the annual budget, rather than running the two as loosely related exercises that happen to share a calendar.


The logic is straightforward once stated plainly. If the long-range plan says the company will invest heavily in a new market next year, and the annual budget doesn't reflect that investment, one of the two documents is wrong, and the organization has no way of knowing which. Allowing the first year of a five-year plan to diverge from the annual budget doesn't create flexibility; it creates two competing versions of what the company intends to do; that ambiguity is exactly what erodes the credibility of both documents with the people who must execute against them.


### Where Management Attention Should Actually Go


If long-range plans and annual budgets are meant to hold steady and rolling forecasts are meant to tell the truth, the most useful thing a leadership team can do with its limited time is watch the gap between the two.[McKinsey's research on adapting budgeting to volatile conditions](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/our-insights/just-in-time-budgeting-for-a-volatile-economy) , a practice the firm has advocated for since it began studying the discipline in depth, describes exactly this model: Leading companies build rolling forecasts specifically to surface gaps against plan early, then have the CFO convene business leaders, the CEO and operating leadership on a fixed cadence to discuss what's driving the gap and what to do about it. The value isn't in the forecast number itself. It's in the conversation the gap forces the organization to have while there's still time to act on it.


That reframes what most performance reviews are for. A review that spends its time relitigating why the forecast differs from last year's actuals is looking backward. A review that asks why the forecast is diverging from the annual plan, and what the organization is going to do to close that gap before it becomes irreversible, is doing the job the whole planning system was built to enable. In practice, that means:


- **Treating small, early gaps as signals worth investigating** , rather than waiting for a variance to become large enough to be undeniable.
- **Separating the conversation about why a gap exists from the conversation about who's accountable for it** , so the discussion produces honest diagnosis rather than defensive explanation.
- **Reserving the most senior time in the room for the gaps tied to the biggest strategic bets** , rather than spreading equal attention across every line item regardless of its size or strategic weight.
- **Deciding explicitly whether to hold the plan, adjust it or reallocate resources** , rather than letting the conversation end in a shared acknowledgment of the gap with no actual decision attached.


### Treating the Three Processes as One System


None of this works if long-range planning, annual budgeting and rolling forecasting are designed, governed and reviewed as three unrelated calendar events that happen to touch the same numbers. The AFP research makes the cost of that fragmentation concrete: Even organizations that have invested heavily in modern planning technology are still stuck with budgeting cycles that haven't gotten any faster, largely because the technology was layered onto a process that was never redesigned to work as a connected system in the first place.


The companies getting more value from planning aren’t necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated forecasting models. They're the ones that have been explicit about what each process is actually for, strategy-led commitment in the long-range plan and annual budget, unbiased reality in the rolling forecast, consistency between the first two, and disciplined attention on the gap between the plan and the forecast, rather than trying to force one process to do a job it was never designed to do.
